description.value: The study investigated brain activation, heart rate variability, and their temporal and predictive relationships during paced breathing and psychosocial stress.

design.value: Each participant underwent a single MRI-scanning session during which they performed a paced-breathing and stress induction task. Brain activation was assessed with block-design fMRI, while heart rate and respiration were continuously monitored.

description.value: 35 healthy participants were recruited through community advertisements; three participants were excluded due to excessive head movement during scanning, leading to a sample size of N = 32.

inclusion_criteria.value: no neurological disorder or head injury

exclusion_criteria.value: excessive head movement during scanning (> 4 mm, ± 3° of rotation)

medical_condition.value: healthy participants; no mental illness history, neurological disorder, or head injury

task_description.value: The task began with 4 min of unpaced breathing, followed by 4 min of normal paced breathing at 10 breaths/min and 4 min of deep-paced breathing at 5.5 breaths/min. Participants then completed the Montreal Imaging Stress Task, involving time-limited arithmetic problems and manipulated negative performance feedback, followed by a 4-min recovery-from-stress block of deep breathing at 5.5 breaths/min.

presentation_software.value: Presentation V18 (Neurobehavioral Systems, Berkeley, Calif., USA)

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to follow a paced breathing exercise. During the Montreal Imaging Stress Task, they had to solve simple arithmetic tasks and submit their response via a response button box.

stimuli.value: Visual breathing cues; simple arithmetic problems; feedback stating “correct,” “incorrect” or “too slow”; and a mock performance bar comparing the participant's performance with an artificially set average performance of 80% success.

task_performance_measures.value: Responses to simple arithmetic tasks submitted via a response button box

instrument.value: Prisma Fit 3-T whole-body MR scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a standard 32-channel head coil

description.value: 40 oblique interleaved slices were acquired parallel to the AC-PC axis using a T2*-sensitive single-shot EPI sequence. A total of 500 images were collected during one single run.

description.value: fMRI data were pre-processed using exclusion of the first four volumes, slice time correction, realignment and unwarping, coregistration of T1 images with the mean T2* images, normalization to MNI space, and smoothing of functional images.

steps.value: Exclusion of first four volumes to account for magnetic field equilibration
Realignment and unwarping to correct for artifacts due to susceptibility-by-movement interactions
Coregistration of T1 images with the mean T2* images
Normalization to MNI space: functional images at 3 mm3 and anatomical images at 1 mm3
Smoothing of functional images with an 8 mm Gaussian kernel

model_settings.value: Natural log-corrected IBI and RMSSD values were compared across experimental blocks; post hoc comparisons used Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference test.

estimator.value: repeated measures ANOVA with Tukey's HSD post hoc test

model_settings.value: A block-design model was constructed with task events modeled using boxcar functions and a 480 s high-pass filter to remove low-frequency noise and signal drift. Individual contrasts included Relaxation, Stress Reactivity, Stress Recovery Specific Relaxation, Post Stress Relaxation, and additional baseline contrasts.

One-sample T-tests were employed for each of the four contrasts of interest. Stress Reactivity results were exclusively masked using stress induction versus unpaced breathing and stress induction versus normal-paced breathing masks, each with a cluster-defining voxel-wise threshold of family-wise error-corrected P < 0.0001.

Two additional GLMs were computed for each participant, one including a regressor for RMSSD values and one including a regressor for IBI values. The time series were resampled at the fMRI TR using a 20 s sliding window shifted by 2.5 s and mean-centered. First-level results with and without the HRV regressors were compared using paired T-tests.
For each of the four contrasts of interest, additional one-sample T-tests included individual PSS or TICS-SCSS scores as regressors of interest.

RMSSD values were modeled as the response variable and brain activation time series from seven a priori ROIs were included as smooth predictor terms. Experimental condition, subjects, and time points were included as parametric terms. Thin plate regression splines were used, smoothing parameters were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood, and subject and condition were included as fixed effects in the final model.

IBI values were modeled as the response variable and brain activation time series from seven a priori ROIs were included as smooth predictor terms. Experimental condition, subjects, and time points were included as parametric terms. Thin plate regression splines were used, smoothing parameters were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood, and subject and condition were included as fixed effects in the final model.

model_type.value: Granger causality analysis using vector autoregressive (VAR) models

model_settings.value: For each participant, ROI time series were extracted as the first eigenvariate of the BOLD signal within each mask, temporally aligned with IBI and RMSSD metrics, and averaged across subjects to obtain group-level time series. Bivariate VAR models were fitted for each HRV-ROI pair, with optimal lag order determined using the Akaike Information Criterion. Significance was assessed using 1,000 permutations of independently shuffled HRV and ROI time series, with Bonferroni correction.

estimator.value: vector autoregressive modeling with permutation-based null distribution

model_settings.value: Two-tailed correlations were used to assess relationships between differences in IBI and RMSSD across experimental conditions and individual PSS, TICS-SCSS, and STAI scores, with P < 0.05.
